claims.text: The initial alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution supersaturated with elements including Mg, Ti, and Zn.
Controlled thermal exposure at 300–500 °C drives decomposition of the metastable solid solution into discrete intermetallic phases.
The transformation proceeds by nucleation of nanoscale Ti- or Zn-rich intermetallic precipitates within the matrix.
Mg-Ti-Zn alloys have a tendency to form intermetallic compounds such as Ti-Zn and Mg-Zn phases.
Slower transformation kinetics produce a fine, evenly dispersed precipitate distribution.
Fine intermetallic precipitates act as nucleation sites for a continuous TiO2-rich oxide layer.
A TiO2-rich surface film enhances passivation and lowers corrosion current density in an Mg-Ti-Zn alloy.
A continuous, adherent TiO2-rich film retains high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Accelerated transformation kinetics produce coarser intermetallic networks.
Coarse intermetallic networks interrupt the continuity of the protective oxide film.
Disruption of oxide-film continuity increases corrosion current density and degrades corrosion resistance.
Disruption of oxide-film continuity increases oxidation mass gain and degrades high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial metastable solid-solution state forms only a transient, incomplete oxide film.
Relative to the initial state, an aged sample with finely dispersed precipitates will have a more continuous oxide film and lower corrosion current density.
The proposed mechanism applies at moderate service temperatures of approximately 300–500 °C and in chloride-containing environments before transformation is complete.
Chloride exposure and high-temperature oxidation conditions promote phase decomposition of the metastable alloy.
After complete transformation, additional degradation mechanisms may dominate behavior.
The precipitation kinetics and critical precipitate size or distribution needed for oxide-film integrity are uncertain and composition- and environment-dependent.
